title: The US Army pushed a 2,700 km road to Alaska in under eight months

cover.alt: Faded colour film still: a bulldozer ploughs through deep snow among snow-laden spruce trees.
cover.credit: US Army Signal Corps · Public domain

body: After Pearl Harbor, the threat of Japanese attacks on the west coast and the Aleutian Islands made the United States want an overland route to Alaska. Canada agreed to a road across its territory on condition that the US paid the full cost. Construction officially began on 9 March 1942, and more than 10,000 soldiers, about a third of them Black, cut through forest and frozen marsh from both ends. The whole route, about 1,700 miles (2,700 km), was finished on 28 October 1942.

slides.alt: Faded colour film: bulldozers grind through deep snow in a spruce forest, one pushing a wall of snow ahead of its blade.
slides.caption: From the US Army’s 1944 film Alaska Highway: bulldozers grind through deep snow in a spruce forest along the route.
slides.credit: US Army Signal Corps · Public domain · excerpt

events.text: Crews meet at Mile 588: Contact Creek

slides.heading: About 1 in 3 of the more than 10,000 soldiers who built it were Black
slides.note: They included the 93rd, 95th and 97th General Service Regiments.

slides.question: On what condition did Canada let the US build the road across its land?
options: The US paid the full cost
It would be torn up after the war
slides.explanation: Canada agreed as long as the United States bore the whole cost of building it.

slides.prompt: In May and June 1943, about 100 miles of the new road became nearly impassable. Why?
slides.answer: The frozen ground beneath it thawed
slides.detail: Thawing permafrost destroyed the layer of plants that held the road together near Burwash Landing and Koidern. Crews fixed it with a corduroy road of logs.
